text: Wilbur Zelinsky (December 21, 1921 – May 4, 2013) was an American cultural geographer who served as a professor emeritus at Pennsylvania State University and is best known for creating the Zelinsky Model of Demographic Transition. Born in Chicago to Russian immigrants Louis Zelinsky and Esther Mastoon, he graduated from Edwin G. Foreman High School. He earned his Bachelor's Degree from the University of California, Berkeley (UC Berkeley) in 1944, his Master's Degree from the University of Madison, Wisconsin, and completed his PhD at UC Berkeley in 1953, studying under Carl Sauer. Zelinsky conducted extensive geographical research on American popular culture, including the diffusion of classical place-names, spatial patterns of personal given names, and the spatial distribution of religious denominations. One of his notable projects examined the influence of personal preference on the spatial character of American society. In the 1960s, he collaborated with Gordon DeJong, Warren Robinson, and Paul Baker to establish a population research center and coordinate an interdisciplinary graduate program in population studies at Penn State, helping to establish the dual-title Graduate Program in Demography. From 1972 to 1973, he served as the first Director of the Population Issues Research Center, which later became the Population Research Institute at Penn State. In 1973, he published The Cultural Geography of the United States, contributing significantly to both population and folk geography. His Theory of First Effective Settlement posits that the dominant culture of a nation is shaped by the first settlers who successfully establish a self-perpetuating society, asserting that these early settlers have a more lasting impact than later waves of immigrants. This theory is further developed by Colin Woodard in his book American Nations. Zelinsky died in his home in State College, Pennsylvania, at the age of 91.
